questions.question: Define migration, distinguish it from circulation, and classify migration along the three axes used in the lesson, giving an example for each category.
questions.expected_answer: Migration is a permanent or semi-permanent change in a person's place of residence. Circulation covers repeated, temporary movements that return home without changing residence — daily commuting, a boarder's weekly cycle, seasonal harvest work — so commuters, tourists and shift workers are not migrants. True migration is classified along three axes. WHERE: internal migration stays within one country, such as moving from Limpopo to Tshwane, with the mover called an in-migrant at the destination and an out-migrant at the origin; international migration crosses a border, and the same person is an emigrant from the country left and an immigrant into the country entered. Internal streams include rural-to-urban (the dominant stream in developing countries, driving urbanisation), urban-to-rural, rural-to-rural (farmworkers moving between districts) and urban-to-urban (leaving East London for Cape Town for a better post). WHY: voluntary migration is chosen, usually for work, wages, study or family; forced migration offers no real choice — flight from war, persecution or disaster — with the ladder of refugee (crossed a border fleeing persecution), asylum seeker (awaiting refugee recognition) and internally displaced person (fleeing danger inside their own country); apartheid removals such as Cato Manor and South End, and relocation into the homelands, were forced movements within a border. HOW LONG: permanent migration intends no return, while temporary migration does — classically the contract mineworkers who spent eleven months on the mines and December at home, a pattern called circular or oscillating migration.

questions.question: Explain the push-pull model of migration, including the four families of factors, intervening obstacles, and the role of perception.
questions.expected_answer: Push factors are the defects of the origin that drive people out; pull factors are the attractions of the destination that draw them in, and every migration involves both. The four families: ECONOMIC — joblessness, poverty wages, shrinking plots and landlessness push, while employment, better pay and the scale of a metropolitan economy pull; economic motives dominate world migration. SOCIAL — weak schools, remote clinics and absent services push, while universities, hospitals, electricity and especially family already settled at the destination pull; settled relatives provide beds, advice and job leads, making each next move cheaper and safer, which is chain migration and explains why streams widen over time. POLITICAL — conflict, persecution, discrimination and instability push; peace, security and rights pull. ENVIRONMENTAL — drought, floods, exhausted soils and climate change push; dependable rain and productive land pull. The decision is weighed against intervening obstacles between the two places — transport costs, distance, visas and border posts, and the emotional cost of leaving family — so migration happens only when expected gain outweighs cost after obstacles are counted. Finally, the decision runs on perception: migrants respond to the destination as imagined from relatives' stories, photos and social media, a picture usually sunnier than reality, which is why streams keep flowing into cities that already have severe unemployment.

questions.question: Using the Eastern Cape to Gauteng stream and the Zimbabwean stream into South Africa, discuss the causes of each migration and evaluate the consequences for both origin and destination.
questions.expected_answer: The Eastern Cape stream has engineered historical roots: the homeland system confined the majority population to poor land in territories such as the former Transkei and Ciskei, while the migrant labour system sent men on eleven-month mine contracts under pass laws that barred their families; when controls ended in the 1990s, families could move together. Pushes are the homeland inheritance — rural unemployment, fragmented plots, thin services; pulls are Gauteng's jobs, schools and hospitals, multiplied by village networks already established there. Consequences: the origin gains remittances and returning skills but loses working-age adults, leaving grandmother-headed households, unploughed fields and a population with a missing middle; the destination gains a young workforce and spending but strains under informal settlement growth, overcrowded services and job competition; the stream stays partly circular, with monthly transfers, December returns and plans to retire home. The Zimbabwean stream was pushed by post-2000 economic collapse — hyperinflation, vanished jobs, decayed services — compounded by political intimidation, and pulled by the region's strongest economy, a shared border and existing networks; over a million Zimbabweans live in South Africa, in a mixed-migration flow of economic migrants, refugees and asylum seekers, alongside older contract-miner streams from Lesotho and Mozambique and refugees and traders from the DRC, Somalia and Ethiopia. Consequences: sending countries gain lifeline remittances but suffer a brain drain of nurses, teachers and artisans; South Africa gains labour, businesses and scarce skills but sees sharpened competition for jobs, housing and services in its poorest areas — pressure that turned into xenophobic violence in 2008 and 2015, at a cost in lives, livelihoods and regional standing that an honest answer must name.
